title: What If an Iron Rod Shot Through Your Skull? A Man Walked Away in 1848 and Lived 12 Years

scenes.text: What if a meter-long iron bar shot through your head? In 1848 a man sat up and talked.
September 13, 1848, Vermont. Foreman Phineas Gage, 25, packs gunpowder with a tamping iron: 1 meter long, 3 centimeters thick, 6 kilos.
The powder ignites. The rod enters under his left cheekbone, exits the top of his skull and lands 25 meters away.
Minutes later he is conscious and speaking. Ten days later doctors expect him to die. Within months he is walking, much of his frontal lobe gone.
His memory and speech are fine. His personality is not. Friends say he is no longer Gage: restless, profane.
He drove stagecoaches in Chile and died of seizures in 1860. Skull and iron sit in a Harvard museum, the case that showed what the frontal lobe does.

description:
What if an iron rod shot through your skull? On 13 September 1848 near Cavendish, Vermont, 25-year-old railroad foreman Phineas Gage was tamping gunpowder when it exploded, driving a tamping iron about 1 metre long, 3.2 cm thick and 6 kg through his left cheek and out the top of his head; it landed about 25 metres away.
Gage was conscious and talking within minutes. Doctors expected him to die days later, yet he recovered within months with his memory and speech intact, having lost much of his left frontal lobe. His physician John Harlow and his friends reported a changed personality, no longer Gage. He later drove stagecoaches in Chile, developed epileptic seizures and died in May 1860, nearly 12 years after the accident. His skull and the iron are displayed at Harvard's Warren Anatomical Museum.
